figures.name: Cyprian of Carthage
figures.dates: born c. 200-210; baptized c. 246; bishop of Carthage 248/249; beheaded 14 September 258
figures.places: Carthage (North Africa, modern Tunisia); hiding near Carthage in 250-251; exile at Curubis 257-258
figures.role: Wealthy teacher of rhetoric turned bishop of Carthage; led the African church through the Decian persecution, a plague and two schisms; martyr
figures.status_note: Saint and martyr in the Catholic Church (feast 16 September, with Pope Cornelius), the Orthodox Church (31 August), and the Anglican and Lutheran calendars. Cautions: his insistence that baptism given by heretics or schismatics is void (so they must be baptized again) was rejected by Pope Stephen and later by the whole Western church; Augustine had to argue against the Donatists who quoted him. 'No salvation outside the Church' is his, and churches read it very differently today. Letter numbers differ between the Ante-Nicene Fathers (ANF, the old Oxford order used by New Advent) and modern editions (Hartel); both are given where they differ.
figures.hook: A rich orator who sold his estates for the poor, he hid from one persecution to steer his church by letter, and when the sword finally came he said 'Thanks be to God' and had his friends give the executioner twenty-five gold coins.

stories.story: As a new believer, before he was even a priest, he sold whole estates and gave the money to the poor. His deacon says he did it 'with premature swiftness of piety'.
stories.source: Pontius the Deacon, Life of Cyprian 2 (Pontius was his deacon and went into exile with him); Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 67 ('gave all his substance to the poor')

stories.story: When the people of Carthage demanded him as bishop, he tried to slip away and give place to older clergy; crowds besieged his house. Some opposed his election; he later forgave them and made them among his closest friends, 'to the astonishment of many'.
stories.source: Pontius, Life of Cyprian 5

stories.story: In the plague of the 250s, when pagans were throwing the sick and dead into the streets, he gathered his people and told them there was nothing wonderful in caring only for their own. They organized care for everyone, pagans included; the poor gave labour instead of money.
stories.source: Pontius, Life of Cyprian 9-10

stories.story: When raiders carried off Christian men and women from Numidia, his church collected one hundred thousand sesterces and sent it to ransom them, with a list of the givers so the captives could pray for them.
stories.source: Cyprian, Epistle 59 (ANF; Hartel 62), sections 1-4

stories.story: Asked whether an actor who had quit the stage but still taught acting could take communion, he said no, not while he kept teaching it; but if the man said he needed the income, the church would feed and clothe him, and if the local church could not afford it, he could come to Carthage and be supported there.
stories.source: Cyprian, Epistle 60 (ANF; Hartel 2)

stories.story: He fled the Decian persecution in 250 and ran his church by letter from hiding. The Roman clergy wrote to Carthage that he had 'acted quite rightly', then pointedly quoted the Good Shepherd and 'the hireling ... sees the wolf coming, and leaves the sheep, and flees'. In 258, told he would be taken to Utica for trial, he hid again, this time so that he could die in Carthage in front of his own people.
stories.source: Epistle 2 (ANF; Hartel 8), from the Roman clergy; Cyprian, Epistle 82 (ANF; Hartel 81)

stories.story: At his trial the proconsul told him to perform the Roman rites and warned him, 'Consult your own interest.' He answered: 'Do what you have been ordered. In a matter so just there is nothing to deliberate.' When the death sentence was read he said, 'Thanks be to God.' He knelt, took off his cloak, told his people to give the executioner twenty-five gold pieces, and tied the blindfold himself; the executioner's hand shook so much he could hardly hold the sword.
stories.source: Acts of Cyprian (Acta Proconsularia) 3-5, the court record; Pontius, Life of Cyprian 18. Own rendering from the Latin (Ruinart's text). An Oxford editor suspected the gold coins were a copyist's addition; Ruinart notes that all the manuscripts he saw have it.

stories.story: An old man who had been his secretary told Jerome that Cyprian never let a day pass without reading Tertullian, and would say, 'Give me the master.'
stories.source: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 53 (second-hand, told to Jerome by Paul of Concordia)

stories.story: Sweating after the walk to his trial, he was offered dry clothes by a soldier who had once been a Christian. He declined: 'We apply medicines to annoyances which probably today will no longer exist.'
stories.source: Pontius, Life of Cyprian 16

temperament.evidence: His deacon: 'His countenance was grave and joyous. Neither was his severity gloomy, nor his affability excessive, but a mingled tempering of both'.
'How mercifully he forgave them, reckoning them afterwards, to the astonishment of many, among his closest and, most intimate friends!'

temperament.trait: Thin-skinned about his authority as bishop
temperament.evidence: To a layman who questioned his standing: 'For what swelling of pride is this, what arrogance of soul, what inflation of mind, to call prelates and priests to one's own recognition'.

temperament.trait: Sharp in controversy, but would not break communion over it
temperament.evidence: He wrote of 'the bitter obstinacy of our brother Stephen', yet opened the council of 256 by asking each bishop's view, 'judging no man, nor rejecting any one from the right of communion, if he should think differently from us.'
temperament.source: Epistle 73 (ANF; Hartel 74) 7; Seventh Council of Carthage, opening address

temperament.trait: Changed his mind, and said so
temperament.evidence: On readmitting the lapsed he moved from a hard line to a more lenient one and defended it: 'Both of which things have been done by me, not without long-balanced and pondered reasons.'

temperament.trait: Trusted dreams and visions for guidance, and knew some mocked him for it
temperament.evidence: 'Although I know that to some men dreams seem ridiculous and visions foolish, yet assuredly it is to such as would rather believe in opposition to the priest, than believe the priest.'

genuine_lines.quote: He can no longer have God for his Father, who has not the Church for his mother.
genuine_lines.work: On the Unity of the Church
genuine_lines.translation: R. E. Wallis, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 5 (1886), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: for custom without truth is the antiquity of error.
genuine_lines.translation: R. E. Wallis, ANF 5 (1886), New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: The whole world is wet with mutual blood; and murder, which in the case of an individual is admitted to be a crime, is called a virtue when it is committed wholesale.
genuine_lines.translation: R. E. Wallis, ANF 5 (1886), New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: They think that they possess, when they are rather possessed; as slaves of their profit, and not lords with respect to their own money, but rather the bond-slaves of their money.
genuine_lines.translation: R. E. Wallis, ANF 5 (1886), New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: who do not speak great things, but live them
genuine_lines.translation: R. E. Wallis, ANF 5 (1886), New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: for God is the hearer, not of the voice, but of the heart.
genuine_lines.translation: R. E. Wallis, ANF 5 (1886), New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: Thanks be to God.
genuine_lines.location: 4 (his answer to the death sentence; Latin 'Deo gratias')
genuine_lines.translation: own rendering from Ruinart's Latin text

genuine_lines.quote: Do what you have been ordered. In a matter so just there is nothing to deliberate.
genuine_lines.location: 3 (reply to the proconsul's 'Consult your own interest')
genuine_lines.translation: own rendering from Ruinart's Latin text
genuine_lines.original: Fac quod tibi praeceptum est. In re tam justa nulla est consultatio.

misattributed.line: "Extra ecclesiam nulla salus" ("Outside the Church there is no salvation") quoted as Cyprian's exact words
misattributed.truth: The idea is his, but his wording is salus extra ecclesiam non est (English ANF: 'there is no salvation out of the Church'; the Latin is as commonly cited and was not checked in a Latin edition here), Epistle 72 (ANF; Hartel 73) 21, in an argument about the baptism of heretics. The neat Latin slogan is a later compression.

misattributed.line: "The Church is a hospital for sinners"
misattributed.truth: No confirmed source in Cyprian or any Father, though it is sometimes pinned on him.

misattributed.line: Icons and stories of 'St Cyprian and St Justina', the magician converted by a Christian virgin
misattributed.truth: That is Cyprian of Antioch, a legendary figure. Gregory of Nazianzus (Oration 24) already merged the two men. Portraits labelled 'Cyprian and Justina' are not Cyprian of Carthage.

misattributed.line: Works printed under his name: On the Public Shows, On the Advantage of Chastity, On Gamblers (De aleatoribus), In Praise of Martyrdom, To Novatian, On Rebaptism
misattributed.truth: Not his. On the Public Shows and On the Advantage of Chastity are now generally assigned to Novatian; the others are anonymous. 'On the Vanity of Idols' is disputed.

misattributed.line: Lines on the 'chair of Peter' from On the Unity of the Church 4
misattributed.truth: Chapter 4 survives in two versions (one stressing Peter's primacy, one not). Many scholars think Cyprian wrote both at different times. Quote with care; do not build a result on it.

opinions.position: Money owns the rich more than they own it; love of property is what made so many deny Christ under persecution.
opinions.side_note: Strongly against attachment to wealth; he himself sold his estates.
opinions.quote: They think that they possess, when they are rather possessed; as slaves of their profit, and not lords with respect to their own money, but rather the bond-slaves of their money.
opinions.translation: R. E. Wallis, ANF 5 (1886), New Advent
opinions.today: Split. Most Christians agree in principle that wealth can enslave, but few accept that ordinary saving is spiritual danger; many secular people see wealth as freedom. Works best paired with his concrete claims below.

opinions.topic: new: leave money to your children or give it away
opinions.position: Do not hoard an inheritance for your children; give it to God through the poor and trust God to guard them. A father who saves for his heirs' earthly estate and not their heavenly one wrongs them twice.
opinions.quote: Assign to Him your wealth which you are saving up for your heirs.
opinions.translation: R. E. Wallis, ANF 5 (1886), New Advent
opinions.today: Sharply split and very personal. Most parents, Christian or not, think leaving something to your children is a duty; a minority (and some Christian givers) would side with him. Excellent quiz material because it is concrete and everyone has a gut answer.

opinions.position: The rich who come to church and give nothing are living off what the poor give.
opinions.quote: You are wealthy and rich, and do you think that you celebrate the Lord's Supper, not at all considering the offering, who come to the Lord's Supper Without a sacrifice, and yet take part of the sacrifice which the poor man has offered?
opinions.translation: R. E. Wallis, ANF 5 (1886), New Advent
opinions.today: Most churchgoers would agree the well-off should give; fewer would say it this bluntly. Better as a reveal line than a statement.

opinions.position: War is murder on a grand scale; calling mass killing a virtue does not make it one.
opinions.side_note: Against the glory of war; he does not discuss whether a Christian may serve as a soldier.
opinions.quote: The whole world is wet with mutual blood; and murder, which in the case of an individual is admitted to be a crime, is called a virtue when it is committed wholesale.
opinions.translation: R. E. Wallis, ANF 5 (1886), New Advent
opinions.today: Split. Pacifists, many progressives and many Anabaptists agree; most people accept some wars as just and honour soldiers. Contrast with Athanasius, who called killing in war 'lawful and praiseworthy'.

opinions.position: Entertainment built on real violence (the gladiator games) trains cruelty in the watchers; the theatre teaches the vices it shows.
opinions.side_note: Against the shows.
opinions.quote: Man is slaughtered that man may be gratified, and the skill that is best able to kill is an exercise and an art.
opinions.translation: R. E. Wallis, ANF 5 (1886), New Advent
opinions.today: Everyone today condemns killing for sport, so the gladiator line alone is one-sided. The live question is his wider claim that what we watch shapes us (violent films, combat sports): people split on that.

opinions.position: In persecution Christ commands his people to flee; running away is not denial, it is waiting for God's time. Later he added: do not hand yourself in either.
opinions.side_note: For flight. He practised it in 250 and was criticised for it; in 258 he hid only so as to die in his own city.
opinions.quote: And therefore the Lord commanded us in the persecution to depart and to flee; and both taught that this should be done, and Himself did it.
opinions.translation: R. E. Wallis, ANF 5 (1886), New Advent
opinions.today: Most people today think escaping danger is sensible; a minority admire staying put at all costs. Among the Fathers the question was live (Tertullian said flight was sin).

opinions.position: Do not provoke the authorities or volunteer yourself for arrest; speak when you are taken, not before.
opinions.side_note: Against volunteer martyrdom.
opinions.quote: nor let any of you stir up any tumult for the brethren, or voluntarily offer himself to the Gentiles.
opinions.translation: R. E. Wallis, ANF 5 (1886), New Advent
opinions.today: Could become 'Standing up for your faith means picking the fight' vs 'Wait until it comes to you'. People split on confrontational activism.

opinions.position: Christians should not mourn their dead in black as if they were lost; the dead are 'sent before', to be missed but not wailed over. Loud grief contradicts what we say we believe.
opinions.side_note: Firmly against open mourning; written in a plague.
opinions.quote: that they should be desired, but not bewailed; that the black garments should not be taken upon us here, when they have already taken upon them white raiment there
opinions.translation: R. E. Wallis, ANF 5 (1886), New Advent
opinions.today: Sharply split. Many people today think grief must be expressed and that 'don't grieve, they're in a better place' is hurtful; some believers still hold his view. Handle with care in a quiz.

opinions.topic: new: does faith protect you from harm
opinions.position: Christians get sick and die in plagues like everyone else; believing was never a promise of a trouble-free life in this world.
opinions.side_note: Against any view that faith makes a believer safe from harm.
opinions.quote: But nevertheless it disturbs some that the power of this Disease attacks our people equally with the heathens, as if the Christian believed for this purpose, that he might have the enjoyment of the world and this life free from the contact of ills
opinions.translation: R. E. Wallis, ANF 5 (1886), New Advent
opinions.today: Good divider: prosperity and healing-focused Christians expect God to protect the faithful; most other Christians and all sceptics side with Cyprian.

opinions.position: Those who denied Christ under persecution can be restored after real, proven repentance; neither slam the door nor wave them through.
opinions.side_note: The middle position, between the lax confessors and Novatian's refusal.
opinions.quote: neither being too ungentle and pertinacious in repelling their repentance; nor, again, being too lax and easy in rashly yielding communion.
opinions.translation: R. E. Wallis, ANF 5 (1886), New Advent
opinions.today: Most people choose the middle in the abstract; the split appears on concrete cases (a leader who betrayed people). Pair with Novatian for a clean contrast.

opinions.position: Not all sins are equal; the idea that they are, and that a serious person should never be moved to pity, is Stoic philosophy, not Christianity.
opinions.quote: The principle of the philosophers and stoics is different, dearest brother, who say that all sins are equal, and that a grave man ought not easily to be moved.
opinions.translation: R. E. Wallis, ANF 5 (1886), New Advent
opinions.today: A strong divider. Many evangelicals say 'all sin is equal before God'; Catholics and Orthodox distinguish grave from lesser sins, and most secular people think some wrongs are far worse than others.

opinions.position: No one can sort the wheat from the weeds in the church now; you are not made guilty by sharing a church with sinners, for each carries only his own sin.
opinions.side_note: Against the pure-church view (Novatian's).
opinions.quote: every one is himself held fast in his own sin; nor can one become guilty for another
opinions.translation: R. E. Wallis, ANF 5 (1886), New Advent
opinions.today: Split. Some people leave churches over other members' sins or scandals; others stay and say the church was always mixed. Real and current.

opinions.topic: new: no salvation outside the Church
opinions.position: You cannot have God as Father without the Church as mother; outside the Church's unity there is no salvation, and even martyrdom outside it does not save.
opinions.quote: He can no longer have God for his Father, who has not the Church for his mother.
opinions.work: On the Unity of the Church
opinions.translation: R. E. Wallis, ANF 5 (1886), New Advent
opinions.today: Strong divider. Most Protestants and non-religious people reject it; traditional Catholics and Orthodox affirm a form of it; many modern Catholics soften it. A plain version ('You can follow Christ without belonging to a church') splits people well.

opinions.position: Bishops may hold different views on a disputed question without cutting each other off; no bishop is a 'bishop of bishops' who can force the others.
opinions.side_note: Said while in open conflict with Pope Stephen.
opinions.quote: judging no man, nor rejecting any one from the right of communion, if he should think differently from us.
opinions.work: The Seventh Council of Carthage (256), Cyprian's opening address
opinions.translation: R. E. Wallis, ANF 5 (1886), New Advent
opinions.today: People split between 'unity matters more than winning the argument' and 'truth matters more than unity'. Note the tension with his hard line on schismatics like Novatian.

opinions.position: Long custom proves nothing; if a practice is not true, its age only makes it an old error.
opinions.side_note: Used against Rome's appeal to tradition on rebaptism.
opinions.quote: for custom without truth is the antiquity of error.
opinions.translation: R. E. Wallis, ANF 5 (1886), New Advent
opinions.today: Split between people who trust inherited ways ('it has lasted for a reason') and those who question them. Pleasingly, a traditionalist bishop said it.

opinions.position: Infants should be baptized as soon as possible, not made to wait even eight days; no one is to be kept from God's grace.
opinions.quote: that by us no one ought to be hindered from baptism and from the grace of God, who is merciful and kind and loving to all.
opinions.translation: R. E. Wallis, ANF 5 (1886), New Advent
opinions.today: A real dividing line among Christians: Catholics, Orthodox, Lutherans, Anglicans and Presbyterians baptize infants; Baptists, Pentecostals and many evangelicals do not. Too churchy for a disguised statement, but a strong reveal.

opinions.topic: new: makeup and altering your looks
opinions.position: Women (married or not) should not colour their hair, eyes or cheeks; it corrupts God's handiwork.
opinions.quote: the work of God and His fashioning and formation ought in no manner to be adulterated, either with the application of yellow color, or with black dust or rouge, or with any kind of medicament which can corrupt the native lineaments.
opinions.translation: R. E. Wallis, ANF 5 (1886), New Advent
opinions.today: Almost no one today objects to ordinary makeup, so as worded it is one-sided. A modern form ('It is wrong to change the body God gave you for looks', e.g. cosmetic surgery) splits people much better.

opinions.topic: new: a job you should quit
opinions.position: If your work teaches others to do wrong, quit it even if you need the money; the church will support you on a plain living.
opinions.side_note: The case was an actor who trained boys for the stage; his objection was to the stage's obscenity and to men playing women.
opinions.quote: his necessity also can be assisted among the rest who are maintained by the support of the Church; if he be content, that is, with very frugal but innocent food.
opinions.translation: R. E. Wallis, ANF 5 (1886), New Advent
opinions.today: The principle ('you should leave a job that makes you do wrong, even if it costs you') splits people: many say you must pay the bills. The church-pays-your-keep half is striking and rarely practised.

opinions.position: Pray in church quietly and with restraint, not with loud, tumbling words; God hears the heart, not the volume.
opinions.quote: for God is the hearer, not of the voice, but of the heart.
opinions.translation: R. E. Wallis, ANF 5 (1886), New Advent
opinions.today: Splits Pentecostal and charismatic worshippers (loud, spontaneous) from liturgical and quiet traditions. Also works outside church: expressive vs reserved people.

opinions.position: Christian prayer is plural: we pray 'our', for the whole people, not just for ourselves.
opinions.quote: Our prayer is public and common; and when we pray, we pray not for one, but for the whole people, because we the whole people are one.
opinions.translation: R. E. Wallis, ANF 5 (1886), New Advent
opinions.today: Many modern believers see faith as a private relationship; Cyprian's communal view splits them. A useful 'my faith is personal' vs 'my faith is ours' item.

opinions.position: He once thought a person could not shed ingrained habits; after baptism he found they could be changed at the root, as a gift of God.
opinions.quote: I used to indulge my sins as if they were actually parts of me, and indigenous to me.
opinions.translation: R. E. Wallis, ANF 5 (1886), New Advent
opinions.today: A good everyday divider: 'People don't really change' vs 'Anyone can change completely'. Both views are common.

opinions.position: A Christian should let no anger or quarrel into his heart at all; he may not return evil for evil or keep hatred.
opinions.side_note: The side that rejects anger altogether, not the side that defends righteous anger.
opinions.quote: he ought to admit neither anger nor discord within his breast, since he must neither return evil for evil, nor bear hatred.
opinions.translation: R. E. Wallis, ANF 5 (1886), New Advent
opinions.today: Split: many people think anger at injustice is healthy and right; others aim to let it go entirely.

opinions.position: Christians, though numerous, do not resist arrest or take revenge; they repay hatred with kindness and leave vengeance to God.
opinions.side_note: Addressed to a hostile pagan magistrate.
opinions.quote: For this reason it is that none of us, when he is apprehended, makes resistance, nor avenges himself against your unrighteous violence, although our people are numerous and plentiful.
opinions.translation: R. E. Wallis, ANF 5 (1886), New Advent
opinions.today: Split: most people accept self-defence and resisting injustice; a minority hold to non-resistance.

opinions.topic: new: care for enemies in a crisis
opinions.position: In the plague, caring only for your own is nothing special; Christians must care for pagans and persecutors too, as God sends sun and rain on all.
opinions.side_note: His words as reported by his deacon Pontius, who was present.
opinions.quote: there was nothing wonderful in our cherishing our own people only with the needed attentions of love
opinions.translation: R. E. Wallis, ANF 5 (1886), New Advent
opinions.today: Most agree in principle; the split shows in hard cases (helping people who hate you, using your group's money on outsiders).

opinions.topic: new: is the world getting worse
opinions.position: The world has grown old and is running down; plagues, wars and failing harvests are signs of its age.
opinions.side_note: Said to a pagan who blamed Christians for the disasters.
opinions.quote: the world has now grown old, and does not abide in that strength in which it formerly stood
opinions.translation: R. E. Wallis, ANF 5 (1886), New Advent
opinions.today: Splits people today almost evenly: 'things are getting worse' vs 'things are getting better'. Very usable.

opinions.position: God still guides the church through dreams and visions; those who laugh at them are really refusing to trust their bishop.
opinions.side_note: For present-day revelation.
opinions.quote: Although I know that to some men dreams seem ridiculous and visions foolish, yet assuredly it is to such as would rather believe in opposition to the priest, than believe the priest.
opinions.translation: R. E. Wallis, ANF 5 (1886), New Advent
opinions.today: Split: charismatic Christians expect God to speak through dreams; many other Christians and all sceptics are wary.

opinions.position: Christians are philosophers in deeds, not in words; they do not talk about great things, they live them.
opinions.side_note: Aimed at pagan philosophers.
opinions.quote: who do not speak great things, but live them
opinions.translation: R. E. Wallis, ANF 5 (1886), New Advent
opinions.today: Nearly everyone agrees in the abstract. Better as a genuine line on the result page than as a statement.

opinions.position: The bishop is the centre of unity: whoever is not with the bishop is not in the Church.
opinions.side_note: High view of church authority.
opinions.quote: the bishop is in the Church, and the Church in the bishop
opinions.translation: R. E. Wallis, ANF 5 (1886), New Advent
opinions.today: Divides Catholics and Orthodox (who agree) from most Protestants and the unchurched. A plain version ('Faith needs leaders you submit to' vs 'No one stands between me and God') works.

sparring.over: Readmitting Christians who had denied the faith, and Novatian's rival election as bishop of Rome; Cyprian called him a schismatic who 'is not a Christian'.
sparring.source: Cyprian, Epistle 51 (ANF; Hartel 55) to Antonianus; On the Unity of the Church

sparring.over: Whether people baptized by heretics must be baptized again (Cyprian: yes; Stephen: no, lay on hands). Cyprian wrote of 'the bitter obstinacy of our brother Stephen'; Firmilian of Caesarea wrote to Cyprian of 'this so open and manifest folly of Stephen'. Stephen threatened to break communion; both died before it was settled.
sparring.source: Cyprian, Epistle 73 (ANF; Hartel 74) to Pompey; Firmilian, Epistle 74 (ANF; Hartel 75); Seventh Council of Carthage (256)

sparring.with: Lucian the confessor and other Carthaginian confessors
sparring.over: Confessors in prison issuing blanket certificates of peace that readmitted the lapsed without penance; Cyprian reported Lucian's conduct to Rome and ruled such certificates worthless without the bishop's review (the ANF heading calls it Lucian's forwardness).
sparring.source: Cyprian, Epistle 22 (ANF; Hartel 27) and the certificate in Epistle 16

sparring.with: Felicissimus, Novatus of Carthage and five presbyters
sparring.over: A faction in Carthage that opposed his election and readmitted the lapsed without him; he excommunicated them.
sparring.source: Cyprian, Epistles 37-39 and 48 (ANF)

sparring.over: A layman who doubted Cyprian was a legitimate bishop and wanted him to clear himself; Cyprian's reply is one of his angriest letters.
sparring.source: Cyprian, Epistle 68 (ANF; Hartel 66)

sparring.with: The Roman clergy (during the vacancy of 250)
sparring.over: His flight in the Decian persecution; their letter to Carthage quoted the hireling who flees. He answered with an account of his withdrawal.
sparring.source: Epistle 2 (ANF; Hartel 8); Cyprian, Epistle 14 (ANF; Hartel 20)

sparring.over: Demetrianus blamed Christians for plague, famine and war; Cyprian blamed the world's age and pagan sin.
sparring.source: Cyprian, An Address to Demetrianus

figures.portraits_note: Avoid anything titled 'Cyprian and Justina' (that is Cyprian of Antioch). The Russian icon 'Cyprian von Karthago2.jpg' on Commons may also be the Antiochene Cyprian; not recommended without checking.

figures.name: Novatian
also_known_as: Novatus (so called in Greek writers such as Eusebius and Socrates, a confusion with Novatus of Carthage)
figures.dates: born c. 200-210; rival bishop of Rome from 251; died c. 258 (Socrates says martyred under Valerian; not certain)
figures.role: Roman presbyter and the first Roman theologian to write major works in Latin; spokesman of the Roman clergy in 250; from 251 rival bishop of Rome against Cornelius and head of a strict church that refused to readmit those who had denied the faith
figures.status_note: Not a saint in any church. Condemned as a schismatic by a Roman synod of sixty bishops (251) and by Cyprian and Dionysius of Alexandria. His teaching on the Trinity was orthodox by the standards of his day (Nicene writers later found parts subordinationist) and his church, the Novatianists, kept the Nicene faith and suffered alongside Catholics under Arian emperors. That church lasted in Rome, Constantinople and Asia Minor into the fifth century and later. Caution: most of his life story comes from his enemy Cornelius, whose letter is hostile and partisan.
figures.hook: In 250 he wrote the Roman church's careful middle-way letter on forgiving Christians who had denied the faith; a year later he led a breakaway church that would not take them back, and (his enemy says) made each communicant swear at the altar never to return to his rival.

stories.story: According to Cornelius, he came to faith after an exorcism, fell gravely ill and was baptized by water poured over him on his sickbed; he never received the bishop's sealing afterwards, and the clergy objected when he was ordained.
stories.source: Cornelius of Rome, letter to Fabius of Antioch, in Eusebius, Church History 6.43.14-17 (hostile witness)

stories.story: During the persecution, Cornelius says, he shut himself in his room, refused the deacons' pleas to come out and help endangered believers, and left in anger, saying he no longer wished to be a presbyter because he admired 'another philosophy'.
stories.source: Eusebius, Church History 6.43.16 (Cornelius, hostile)

stories.story: He wrote the Roman clergy's letter to Cyprian in 250 and read it aloud himself: no hasty readmission of those who had lapsed, a council once a bishop was chosen, and peace for the dying who truly repented. Cyprian later threw this back at him.
stories.source: Epistle 30 (ANF; Hartel 30), and Cyprian, Epistle 51 (ANF; Hartel 55) 5: 'Novatian then writing, and reciting with his own voice what he had written'

stories.story: After Cornelius was elected in 251, Novatian had himself consecrated by three bishops from small Italian towns. Cornelius claims they were brought to Rome on a pretext and consecrated him 'by the tenth hour, when they had become drunk and sick'.
stories.source: Eusebius, Church History 6.43.8-9 (Cornelius, hostile)

stories.story: Cornelius says that at communion Novatian held each person's hands in his own and would not let go until they swore: 'Swear to me by the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ that you will never forsake me and turn to Cornelius.'
stories.source: Eusebius, Church History 6.43.18-19 (Cornelius, hostile)

stories.story: Dionysius of Alexandria wrote to him: if you were made bishop against your will, prove it by stepping down; 'it were better to suffer everything, rather than divide the Church of God'.
stories.source: Eusebius, Church History 6.45

stories.story: His movement outlived him. At Nicaea (325) the Novatianist bishop Acesius explained that people who sinned gravely after baptism should repent and hope for pardon from God, not from the priest. Constantine replied: 'Place a ladder, Acesius, and climb alone into heaven.'
stories.source: Socrates, Church History 1.10 (from an old eyewitness he knew)

stories.story: When the Arian bishop Macedonius ordered their church in Constantinople destroyed, Novatianists (with Catholics helping) took it apart themselves, men, women and children carrying tiles, stones and timber across the water to Sycae, and rebuilt it; under Julian they carried it back and named it Anastasia, 'Resurrection'.
stories.source: Socrates, Church History 2.38

temperament.trait: Polished, learned, proud of his philosophy (by his enemies' account)
temperament.evidence: Cyprian: 'Although he may boast himself, and announce his philosophy or eloquence with lofty words, yet he who has not maintained brotherly love or ecclesiastical unity has lost even what he previously had been.'
Cornelius: 'a long time ago this remarkable man desired the episcopate, but kept this ambitious desire to himself and concealed it'.

temperament.trait: Severe, yet in his own letter of 250 he aims for a middle course
temperament.evidence: 'take anxious care that neither ungodly men should praise our smooth facility, nor truly penitent men accuse our severity as cruel.'
temperament.source: Epistle 30 (ANF; Hartel 30) 8, written by Novatian for the Roman clergy

temperament.evidence: On Christians who drink before breakfast: 'still fasting and already drunk, not running to the tavern, but carrying the tavern about with them'.
Writing from absence, he calls the day their letters arrive among his happiest: 'for what else is there now to make me more joyous?'

genuine_lines.quote: Let them indeed knock at the doors, but assuredly let them not break them down
genuine_lines.work: Epistle 30 (ANF; Hartel 30), the Roman clergy to Cyprian, written by Novatian
genuine_lines.translation: R. E. Wallis, ANF 5 (1886), New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: This is not to cure, but, if we wish to speak the truth, to slay.
genuine_lines.translation: R. E. Wallis, ANF 5 (1886), New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: He has prepared heaven, but He has also prepared hell.
genuine_lines.translation: R. E. Wallis, ANF 5 (1886), New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: Moreover, we can in some degree be conscious of Him in silence, but we cannot in discourse unfold Him as He is.
genuine_lines.translation: R. E. Wallis, ANF 5 (1886), New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: for luxury is inimical to holiness.
genuine_lines.translation: R. E. Wallis, ANF 5 (1886), New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: What theatre built by human hands could ever be compared to such works as these?
genuine_lines.work: On the Public Shows (De spectaculis; printed among Cyprian's works, now generally assigned to Novatian)
genuine_lines.translation: R. E. Wallis, ANF 5 (1886), CCEL

genuine_lines.quote: To have vanquished pleasure is the greatest pleasure
genuine_lines.work: On the Advantage of Chastity (De bono pudicitiae; printed among Cyprian's works, now generally assigned to Novatian)
genuine_lines.translation: R. E. Wallis, ANF 5 (1886), CCEL

misattributed.line: On the Trinity quoted as a work of Tertullian or Cyprian
misattributed.truth: It is Novatian's. Jerome (Lives of Illustrious Men 70) calls it 'a sort of epitome of the work of Tertullian, which many mistakenly ascribe to Cyprian'; manuscripts carried it with Tertullian's works.

misattributed.line: On the Public Shows and On the Advantage of Chastity quoted as Cyprian's
misattributed.truth: Transmitted under Cyprian's name and printed so in the ANF, but now generally assigned to Novatian on grounds of style (both are letters from a bishop absent from his flock). Treat the attribution as probable, not certain.

misattributed.line: 'Novatus' in Eusebius, Socrates and other Greek writers
misattributed.truth: They mean Novatian. The real Novatus was a Carthaginian presbyter who opposed Cyprian and then joined Novatian's party in Rome (Cyprian, Epistle 48 ANF).

misattributed.line: 'Novatian taught that God cannot forgive those who denied Christ'
misattributed.truth: Overstated. As his rule is reported, the church should not readmit them to communion but should urge them to repent and 'leave the pardoning of their offense to God, who has the power to forgive all sin' (Socrates, Church History 4.28). Cyprian's objection was that this made repentance pointless.

misattributed.line: A catacomb inscription to 'the most blessed martyr Novatian'
misattributed.truth: An inscription naming a martyr Novatian was found in Rome in the twentieth century and is sometimes linked to him; the identification is disputed (secondary-only; not checked in a primary source here).

opinions.position: In 250 (his own words): Christians who denied the faith must not be rushed back; they may knock at the church's door but not break it down; those truly repentant and dying may be given peace, and the rest wait for a council.
opinions.side_note: At this date the middle position, close to Cyprian's. His later view (below) was the hard one.
opinions.quote: Let them indeed knock at the doors, but assuredly let them not break them down
opinions.work: Epistle 30 (ANF; Hartel 30), written by Novatian for the Roman clergy
opinions.translation: R. E. Wallis, ANF 5 (1886), New Advent
opinions.today: Most people accept 'forgiveness has to be earned and proven'. A contrast with 'forgive and restore quickly' splits people.

opinions.position: From 251: the church may not readmit to communion anyone who sacrificed to idols; urge them to repent for life and leave their pardon to God.
opinions.side_note: The hard side. A change from his 250 letter.
opinions.quote: they should not admit to the sacred mysteries those who had sacrificed; but exhorting them to repentance, leave the pardoning of their offense to God, who has the power to forgive all sin.
opinions.work: Socrates, Church History (reporting Novatian's circular letters)
opinions.translation: A. C. Zenos, NPNF second series vol. 2 (1890), New Advent
opinions.today: Few people today would bar someone from church for life, but many would bar a leader who betrayed people from ever leading again. Recast as 'some betrayals should end your place in a community for good' and people split.

opinions.position: The church should be a community of the pure; his followers took the name Cathari ('the Pure') and would not share communion with churches that readmitted apostates.
opinions.side_note: The pure-church side. His own words on it do not survive; this is how his opponents and later historians describe the movement.
opinions.quote: became leader of the heresy of those who, in the pride of their imagination, call themselves Cathari.
opinions.translation: A. C. McGiffert, NPNF second series vol. 1 (1890), New Advent
opinions.today: Split: some people want a church or group that holds members to a high standard and expels those who fall; others want a mixed, forgiving community.

opinions.topic: new: ordering a wrong is as bad as doing it
opinions.position: Those who bought a certificate saying they had sacrificed, without actually sacrificing, are as guilty as those who did; whoever orders or consents to a wrong shares the crime.
opinions.side_note: Aimed at the 'libellatici' who bribed officials for false certificates.
opinions.quote: For he is not guiltless of wickedness who has bidden it to be done
opinions.translation: R. E. Wallis, ANF 5 (1886), New Advent
opinions.today: Good divider: 'paying someone to cut a corner for you is as bad as doing it yourself' vs 'the one who does the deed carries the blame'. Everyday and disguised.

opinions.topic: new: big decisions need many voices
opinions.position: A judgment affecting many people should be made by many people (bishops, clergy, confessors and faithful laity together), or it will not stand.
opinions.quote: since that cannot be a firm decree which shall not appear to have had the consent of very many.
opinions.translation: R. E. Wallis, ANF 5 (1886), New Advent
opinions.today: Split between people who prefer consensus and those who prefer one clear leader deciding. Ironic, given how he then acted.

opinions.position: God is merciful, but He also exacts obedience; heaven and hell are both real and both prepared by God.
opinions.side_note: Against universal salvation.
opinions.quote: He has prepared heaven, but He has also prepared hell.
opinions.translation: R. E. Wallis, ANF 5 (1886), New Advent
opinions.today: Split: most traditional Christians affirm hell; a growing number of Christians and most non-religious people doubt it.

opinions.position: God is greater than any thought or word; we can sense Him somewhat in silence, but speech can never describe Him as He is.
opinions.side_note: For silence as the truer way toward God.
opinions.quote: Moreover, we can in some degree be conscious of Him in silence, but we cannot in discourse unfold Him as He is.
opinions.translation: R. E. Wallis, ANF 5 (1886), New Advent
opinions.today: Contemplatives and many spiritual-but-not-religious people agree; people who value clear doctrine and words about God lean the other way. Surprising from a man remembered as a hardliner.

opinions.position: God made the world not only useful but beautiful on purpose; He coloured the flowers for the pleasure of our eyes.
opinions.side_note: For creation as good and meant to be enjoyed.
opinions.quote: lest He should not also provide for the very delights of the eyes, He has clothed all things with the various colors of the flowers for the pleasure of the beholders.
opinions.translation: R. E. Wallis, ANF 5 (1886), New Advent
opinions.today: Most believers agree; the question 'is beauty in nature meant for us or just a by-product?' splits believers from many sceptics. Lovely reveal line.

opinions.position: God made humans alone of all creatures free, because the image of God should not be a slave; He gave a law so that freedom would not run wild.
opinions.quote: And when He had given him all things for his service, He willed that he alone should be free.
opinions.translation: R. E. Wallis, ANF 5 (1886), New Advent
opinions.today: Split: many believe in real free will; strict Calvinists and many scientists and philosophers doubt it.

opinions.topic: new: does fear make people good
opinions.position: God's anger is not a vice but medicine; people who ignore reason need fear to move them toward a good life.
opinions.quote: For fear is necessary for those who want the motive to a virtuous life, that they who have forsaken reason may at least be moved by terror.
opinions.translation: R. E. Wallis, ANF 5 (1886), New Advent
opinions.today: Strong everyday divider (parenting, policing, preaching): 'some people only behave out of fear of consequences' vs 'fear never makes anyone truly good'.

opinions.position: Christian freedom about food is not permission for luxury; fasting and self-restraint still matter, and heavy eating and drinking dull prayer.
opinions.side_note: Against indulgence; not against eating any particular food.
opinions.quote: But from the fact that liberty of meats is granted to us, it does not of necessity follow that luxury is allowed us; nor because the Gospel has dealt with us very liberally, has it taken away continency.
opinions.translation: R. E. Wallis, ANF 5 (1886), New Advent
opinions.today: Split: 'good food and drink are gifts to enjoy freely' vs 'indulgence dulls you, keep it plain'.

opinions.position: No food makes you holy or unholy; God is not worshipped by what goes into the stomach but by faith, innocence and truth.
opinions.side_note: He still forbade food offered to idols (chapter 7).
opinions.quote: God rejoices in our faith alone, in our innocency alone, in our truth alone, in our virtues alone.
opinions.translation: R. E. Wallis, ANF 5 (1886), New Advent
opinions.today: Most Christians agree; Orthodox and Catholic fasting rules, Adventists and many religious people keep food rules. Moderate splitter.

opinions.position: The Old Testament food laws are spiritual: the forbidden animals stand for human vices (the swan for pride, the sea-mew for a loose tongue), so read them spiritually, not literally.
opinions.side_note: For the spiritual, allegorical sense.
opinions.quote: if, avoiding blasphemy, they confess it to be spiritual, let them read it spiritually.
opinions.translation: R. E. Wallis, ANF 5 (1886), New Advent
opinions.today: Splits literal readers of Scripture from symbolic readers. Note: the treatise is polemic against Jewish practice; handle with care.

opinions.position: Christians must not attend the public shows even though no verse names them; the shows grew from idolatry. The Christian's true show is the sky, the sea and the works of God.
opinions.side_note: Against the shows. Attribution to Novatian is the scholarly majority view, not certain.
opinions.quote: What theatre built by human hands could ever be compared to such works as these?
opinions.translation: R. E. Wallis, ANF 5 (1886), CCEL
opinions.today: The modern form ('nature beats any screen', or 'if the Bible doesn't forbid it, it's fine') splits people well. He explicitly rejects the second argument in section 2.

opinions.position: The greatest pleasure is mastering pleasure; the man who conquers his own desires is stronger than one who conquers an enemy.
opinions.side_note: For self-mastery over enjoyment. Attribution probable.
opinions.quote: To have vanquished pleasure is the greatest pleasure
opinions.work: On the Advantage of Chastity (De bono pudicitiae)
opinions.translation: R. E. Wallis, ANF 5 (1886), CCEL
opinions.today: Split: disciplined and ascetic people agree; 'enjoy life, you only live once' people do not.

opinions.position: Chastity has three ranks: virgins first, then the married who choose continence, then faithful marriage; all are honourable, but virginity is higher.
opinions.side_note: Ranks celibacy above marriage. Attribution probable.
opinions.quote: But chastity maintains the first rank in virgins, the second in those who are continent, the third in the case of wedlock. Yet in all it is glorious, with all its degrees.
opinions.work: On the Advantage of Chastity (De bono pudicitiae)
opinions.translation: R. E. Wallis, ANF 5 (1886), CCEL
opinions.today: Most people today, including most Protestants, reject ranking celibacy above marriage; traditional Catholics and Orthodox keep a form of it. One-sided among the Fathers.

sparring.over: The see of Rome and the readmission of the lapsed; Cornelius's letter to Fabius of Antioch is a savage portrait of him.
sparring.source: Eusebius, Church History 6.43

sparring.over: The lapsed and the schism; Cyprian refused Novatian's envoys, wrote that 'he who is not in the Church of Christ is not a Christian', and wrote On the Unity of the Church with Novatian's schism in view.
sparring.source: Cyprian, Epistles 40-51 (ANF), esp. 51 (Hartel 55)

sparring.over: Urged him to resign rather than divide the church; later wrote that Novatian had 'calumniated our most compassionate Lord Jesus Christ as unmerciful'.
sparring.source: Eusebius, Church History 6.45 and 7.8

sparring.with: An anonymous bishop (the treatise To Novatian, c. 255)
sparring.over: A tract arguing that the lapsed can be restored.
sparring.source: A Treatise Against the Heretic Novatian, ANF 5

sparring.with: Pacian of Barcelona (after his death, against the Novatianist Sympronian)
sparring.over: Whether the church can forgive grave sins after baptism; Pacian's famous 'Christian is my name, but Catholic my surname' is from this exchange.
sparring.source: Pacian, Letter 1 to Sympronian (C. H. Collyns translation, 1842)

figures.portraits_note: No ancient or medieval portrait of Novatian is known, and none was found on Wikimedia Commons. The result page will need a non-portrait image (for example a view of third-century Rome or a manuscript page of On the Trinity).

figures.name: Athanasius of Alexandria
figures.dates: born c. 296-298; deacon and secretary at the Council of Nicaea 325; bishop of Alexandria 328-373; died 2 May 373
figures.places: Alexandria; exiles in Trier (335-337) and Rome (339-346); hiding in the Egyptian desert and in Alexandria (356-362, 362-363, 365-366)
figures.role: Bishop of Alexandria and the leading defender of the Council of Nicaea's teaching that the Son is fully God; biographer of Antony; exiled five times by four emperors
figures.status_note: Saint in the Catholic Church (Doctor of the Church, feast 2 May), the Orthodox Church (18 January and 2 May), the Coptic Church ('the Apostolic'), and the Anglican and Lutheran calendars. Cautions: his writing against opponents is savage (he calls them 'madmen' and the emperor a forerunner of Antichrist); councils convicted him of violence, and a papyrus letter of 335 (published by H. I. Bell in 1924) records his supporters beating Melitian monks, though how far he directed it is debated (secondary-only). The Athanasian Creed is not his.
figures.hook: Exiled five times by four emperors, he once escaped a boat of pursuers on the Nile by turning around and rowing straight at them; when they asked how far off Athanasius was, he said: not far.

stories.story: As a boy he played at church with other children on the day of the martyr-bishop Peter; he was the 'bishop' and baptized the others. Bishop Alexander saw them, questioned them, and took Athanasius into the church to be educated.
stories.source: Socrates, Church History 1.15, citing Rufinus (Socrates adds that it is not improbable)

stories.story: At the Council of Tyre (335) he was accused of murdering the Melitian bishop Arsenius and cutting off his hand for magic; the accusers even produced a hand. He brought in a cloaked man, asked who knew Arsenius, uncovered one hand, then after a pause the other, and said: 'Arsenius, as you see, is found to have two hands: let my accusers show the place whence the third was cut off.'
stories.source: Socrates, Church History 1.29; Athanasius tells the Arsenius affair himself in Apology against the Arians 63-72

stories.story: Constantine wrote threatening to depose him if he refused communion to Arius; he refused. Later his enemies told the emperor he had threatened to stop the grain ships from Alexandria to Constantinople, and Constantine exiled him to Trier without a hearing.
stories.source: Athanasius, Apology against the Arians 59 and 87

stories.story: On the night of 8-9 February 356 more than five thousand soldiers surrounded his church during a vigil. He sat on his bishop's chair, had a deacon read Psalm 136 with the people answering 'For His mercy endures for ever', and refused to leave until the people had gone. Monks finally dragged him out, and he slipped past the soldiers in the dark.
stories.source: Athanasius, Defence of his Flight 24

stories.story: Julian the Apostate ordered him out of Egypt and wrote, furious, that he 'has had the audacity to baptise Greek women of rank' during Julian's reign. Athanasius told his friends, 'it is but a small cloud which will soon pass away' (Julian died within the year).
stories.source: Julian, Letter 46 (W. C. Wright, Loeb 1923); Socrates, Church History 3.14

stories.story: Fleeing up the Nile with Julian's officer close behind, he ordered his boat turned round to row back toward Alexandria. The pursuer asked the passing boat, 'How far off is Athanasius?' 'Not far,' said Athanasius, and the officer hurried on upriver.
stories.source: Theodoret, Church History 3.5; also Socrates 3.14 (where his companions give the answer)

stories.story: In 365, to avoid being blamed for riots, he hid for four months in his family's tomb until the emperor, faced with an angry city, let him return.
stories.source: Socrates, Church History 4.13

stories.story: He had been Antony's attendant as a young man and 'poured water on his hands'. The dying Antony left him one sheepskin and 'the garment whereon I am laid, which he himself gave me new, but which with me has grown old.'
stories.source: Athanasius, Life of Antony, prologue and 91

temperament.evidence: Gregory of Nazianzus: 'gentle, free from anger, sympathetic, sweet in words, sweeter in disposition'.

temperament.trait: Immovable to enemies, drawing to friends
temperament.evidence: 'for to those who assailed him he was adamant, and to those at variance a magnet'.
Julian: 'for I am informed that the man is a clever rascal'; 'But if this leader is not even a man but only a contemptible puppet'.
temperament.source: Julian, Letter 47, to the Alexandrians (W. C. Wright, 1923)

temperament.trait: Ferocious polemicist, diplomatic when it served
temperament.evidence: To Constantius he wrote as 'most religious Augustus' (Apology to Constantius 1); to the monks he asked of the same emperor, 'Now what is yet wanting to make him Antichrist?'
temperament.source: Apology to Constantius 1; History of the Arians 77

temperament.evidence: 'For the more I desired to write, and endeavoured to force myself to understand the Divinity of the Word, so much the more did the knowledge thereof withdraw itself from me'.

temperament.trait: Stood with his people under threat
temperament.evidence: In the raid of 356: 'saying that it was better that my safety should be endangered, than that any of them should receive hurt.'

genuine_lines.quote: For He was made man that we might be made God
genuine_lines.work: On the Incarnation of the Word
genuine_lines.translation: A. Robertson, NPNF second series vol. 4 (1892), New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: For the truth is not preached with swords or with darts, nor by means of soldiers; but by persuasion and counsel.
genuine_lines.translation: M. Atkinson and A. Robertson, NPNF second series vol. 4 (1892), New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: for the crown is given not according to position, but according to action.
genuine_lines.translation: A. Robertson, NPNF second series vol. 4 (1892), New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: For although it be impossible to comprehend what God is, yet it is possible to say what He is not.
genuine_lines.translation: NPNF second series vol. 4 (1892), New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: Arsenius, as you see, is found to have two hands: let my accusers show the place whence the third was cut off.
genuine_lines.work: Socrates, Church History (reporting his words at Tyre)
genuine_lines.translation: A. C. Zenos, NPNF second series vol. 2 (1890), New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: Let us retire for a little while, friends; it is but a small cloud which will soon pass away.
genuine_lines.work: Socrates, Church History (reporting his words on Julian's edict)
genuine_lines.translation: A. C. Zenos, NPNF second series vol. 2 (1890), New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: And it seems to me that for the one who sings them, these words become like a mirror, so that he sees himself in them and the movements of his own soul, and, having perceived them, speaks them out.
genuine_lines.work: Letter to Marcellinus on the Psalms
genuine_lines.translation: own rendering from the Greek (TLG text posted by Documenta Catholica Omnia); the usual English (CSMV, 1953) is copyrighted
genuine_lines.original: Καί μοι δοκεῖ τῷ ψάλλοντι γίνεσθαι τούτους ὥσπερ εἴσοπτρον, εἰς τὸ κατανοεῖν καὶ αὐτὸν ἐν αὐτοῖς καὶ τὰ τῆς ἑαυτοῦ ψυχῆς κινήματα, καὶ οὕτως αἰσθόμενον ἀπαγγέλλειν αὐτούς.

misattributed.line: The Athanasian Creed (Quicunque vult: 'Whosoever will be saved...')
misattributed.truth: Not by Athanasius. It is a Latin text from the West, generally dated to the late fifth or sixth century; it was named after him because it defends the faith he fought for.
A later Latin tag about him, not his words and not found in any fourth-century source.

misattributed.line: 'They have the premises, but you have the apostolic faith ... Even if Catholics faithful to Tradition are reduced to a handful, they are the ones who are the true Church'
misattributed.truth: Circulates on traditionalist websites as a 'Letter to his flock' with no edition cited. It is not among his letters in NPNF, and the phrase 'Catholics faithful to Tradition' is modern polemical wording. Unverified; do not use.

misattributed.line: Works in his corpus such as Questions to Antiochus and the two books Against Apollinaris
misattributed.truth: Spurious or doubtful. The Life of Antony was once questioned too, but most scholars accept it as his.

opinions.position: Fleeing persecution is commanded and practised by Christ and the saints; hide when hunted, do not rashly tempt God, and stand firm when you are caught. If fleeing is bad, persecuting is far worse.
opinions.side_note: For flight; he fled many times and wrote this defence against charges of cowardice.
opinions.quote: And to all men generally, even to us, is this law given, to flee when persecuted, and to hide when sought after, and not rashly tempt the Lord
opinions.translation: M. Atkinson and A. Robertson, NPNF second series vol. 4 (1892), New Advent
opinions.today: Most people see escaping danger as sensible; a minority admire standing your ground whatever the cost.

opinions.position: If you are called to lead, you may not hide from it: before, you lived for yourself; after, you live for the people in your care. Refusing out of humility or fear lets unfit people take the post.
opinions.side_note: For accepting office. Written to a monk who fled after being elected bishop.
opinions.quote: while before your election you lived to yourself, after it, you live for your flock.
opinions.translation: A. Robertson, NPNF second series vol. 4 (1892), New Advent
opinions.today: Everyday form: 'If people ask you to lead, you have a duty to say yes' vs 'Never take on a role you don't want'. Splits well.

opinions.position: Holiness is not tied to your role: there are bishops who fast and monks who eat, married monks and celibate bishops; God rewards what you do, not where you stand.
opinions.quote: for the crown is given not according to position, but according to action.
opinions.translation: A. Robertson, NPNF second series vol. 4 (1892), New Advent
opinions.today: Nearly everyone agrees; one-sided. Best as a reveal line.

opinions.position: The monk's life in the desert, as Antony lived it, is a sufficient pattern of holiness; but when the church calls a monk to serve, he must leave solitude (see Dracontius).
opinions.side_note: Honours solitude, but puts service above it when called.
opinions.quote: for monks the life of Antony is a sufficient pattern of discipline.
opinions.translation: H. Ellershaw, NPNF second series vol. 4 (1892), New Advent
opinions.today: Splits introverts who long for withdrawal from those who think faith is proven in public service.

opinions.position: Truth must never be spread by force; Christ knocks and waits, only the devil breaks down doors. Coercion in religion is the mark of a false cause.
opinions.side_note: Against state coercion in religion. Written when the emperor was using troops against his party; he did not live under a pro-Nicene emperor who coerced others.
opinions.quote: For the truth is not preached with swords or with darts, nor by means of soldiers; but by persuasion and counsel.
opinions.translation: M. Atkinson and A. Robertson, NPNF second series vol. 4 (1892), New Advent
opinions.today: Almost everyone agrees religion should not be forced, so it is one-sided today; but among the Fathers it contrasts sharply with the later Augustine.

opinions.position: Rulers have no authority over the church's judgments; councils never needed the emperor's consent and emperors should not run church affairs.
opinions.side_note: For the church's independence from the state.
opinions.quote: When did a judgment of the Church receive its validity from the Emperor?
opinions.translation: M. Atkinson and A. Robertson, NPNF second series vol. 4 (1892), New Advent
opinions.today: Split in modern form: 'Churches should stay out of politics and governments out of churches' vs close ties between faith and national life (state churches, Christian nationalism).

opinions.position: Killing is wrong, yet killing the enemy in war is lawful and even praiseworthy; the same act can be wrong or right depending on circumstance.
opinions.side_note: For the lawfulness of war. Balance: in On the Incarnation 52 he also celebrates barbarians who, hearing Christ, 'instead of fighting they turn to husbandry'.
opinions.quote: it is not right to kill, yet in war it is lawful and praiseworthy to destroy the enemy
opinions.translation: A. Robertson, NPNF second series vol. 4 (1892), New Advent
opinions.today: Split: most people accept that killing in a just war is right; pacifists disagree. Direct contrast with Cyprian's 'murder ... is called a virtue when it is committed wholesale'.

opinions.position: Nothing natural in the body is unclean or sinful, since God made it all; defilement comes only from sin you choose.
opinions.side_note: Written to calm monks anxious about involuntary bodily functions.
opinions.quote: All things made by God are beautiful and pure, for the Word of God has made nothing useless or impure.
opinions.translation: A. Robertson, NPNF second series vol. 4 (1892), New Advent
opinions.today: Most people agree today; useful against guilt-heavy views of the body. Somewhat one-sided.

opinions.position: Marriage is honourable and blameless, the ordinary road; virginity is the 'angelic' road with greater rewards (a hundredfold against thirtyfold).
opinions.side_note: Ranks virginity above marriage, but defends marriage against those who called it unclean.
opinions.quote: Now if a man choose the way of the world, namely marriage, he is not indeed to blame; yet he will not receive such great gifts as the other.
opinions.translation: A. Robertson, NPNF second series vol. 4 (1892), New Advent
opinions.today: Most people today, including most Protestants, reject ranking celibacy higher; traditional Catholics and Orthodox keep a form of it.

opinions.position: God made the world orderly so that people who cannot see Him could know Him from His works.
opinions.side_note: For natural knowledge of God through creation.
opinions.quote: He so ordered Creation that although He is by nature invisible He may yet be known by His works.
opinions.translation: A. Robertson, NPNF second series vol. 4 (1892), New Advent
opinions.today: Split: many believers feel nature points to God; sceptics see only nature. A plain version ('Looking at nature, I feel there must be a Maker') splits well.

opinions.position: The psalms are sung to melody not for the pleasure of a nice sound but because the melody expresses and trains a harmony in the soul; simple believers who think it is for the ear's delight are mistaken.
opinions.side_note: Music in worship is for the soul's order, not for enjoyment.
opinions.quote: So the psalms are not sung to a melody out of a zeal for pleasant sound; the melody is a sign of the harmony of the thoughts in the soul.
opinions.work: Letter to Marcellinus on the Psalms
opinions.translation: own rendering from the Greek (TLG text posted by Documenta Catholica Omnia); the usual English (CSMV, 1953) is copyrighted
opinions.original: Τὸ ἄρα μετὰ μέλους λέγεσθαι τοὺς ψαλμοὺς οὐκ ἔστιν εὐφωνίας σπουδὴ, ἀλλὰ τεκμήριον τῆς ἁρμονίας τῶν ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ λογισμῶν.
opinions.today: Split: many worshippers value music because it moves and delights them; others say beautiful music in church is a distraction unless it serves the words.

opinions.topic: new: the Psalms as your own words
opinions.position: Other Scripture you read as other people's words; the Psalms you can pray as your own, and they show you your own soul like a mirror.
opinions.side_note: Links to the site's Psalm quiz and 'How to pray the Psalms' article.
opinions.quote: And it seems to me that for the one who sings them, these words become like a mirror, so that he sees himself in them and the movements of his own soul, and, having perceived them, speaks them out.
opinions.work: Letter to Marcellinus on the Psalms
opinions.translation: own rendering from the Greek (TLG text posted by Documenta Catholica Omnia)
opinions.original: Καί μοι δοκεῖ τῷ ψάλλοντι γίνεσθαι τούτους ὥσπερ εἴσοπτρον, εἰς τὸ κατανοεῖν καὶ αὐτὸν ἐν αὐτοῖς καὶ τὰ τῆς ἑαυτοῦ ψυχῆς κινήματα, καὶ οὕτως αἰσθόμενον ἀπαγγέλλειν αὐτούς.
opinions.today: Mostly agreeable to believers; the everyday form ('I pray best in other people's words' vs 'in my own words') splits people well.

opinions.position: No one can grasp what God is; the harder he tried to understand, the more it slipped away. But we can know what God is not, and that is enough to reject error.
opinions.side_note: Humility about knowledge of God, combined with firm rejection of error.
opinions.quote: For although it be impossible to comprehend what God is, yet it is possible to say what He is not.
opinions.translation: NPNF second series vol. 4 (1892), New Advent
opinions.today: Splits people who think God can be clearly known and defined from those who stress mystery.

opinions.position: When people clearly mean the same thing, stop quarrelling over the terms they use; welcome them and agree in substance.
opinions.side_note: Surprising from the man who fought decades for one word (homoousios); here he accepts different wording for the same faith.
opinions.quote: not to enquire further into each other's opinions, nor to fight about words to no useful purpose, nor to go on contending with the above phrases, but to agree in the mind of piety.
opinions.work: Tome to the People of Antioch (362)
opinions.translation: H. Ellershaw, NPNF second series vol. 4 (1892), New Advent
opinions.today: Split between people who think exact wording matters a great deal and those who care only about the meaning. Works in everyday form.

opinions.position: Those who invented heresy and were condemned by a council may not be admitted to communion, even if the emperor orders it.
opinions.side_note: Hard line on teachers of heresy (not on ordinary sinners).
opinions.quote: it was not right that those who had invented heresy contrary to the truth, and had been anathematized by the Ecumenical Council, should be admitted to communion
opinions.translation: M. Atkinson and A. Robertson, NPNF second series vol. 4 (1892), New Advent
opinions.today: Split: 'some beliefs should get you removed from a church' vs 'churches should include people who believe differently'.

opinions.position: Clergy who went along with heresy under force and fear should be pardoned and even keep their posts; its leaders may be pardoned on repentance but not serve as clergy.
opinions.side_note: The lenient middle, which provoked Lucifer of Cagliari's hardliners.
opinions.quote: in the case of men not deliberate in impiety, but drawn away by necessity and violence, that they should not only receive pardon, but should occupy the position of clergy
opinions.translation: A. Robertson, NPNF second series vol. 4 (1892), New Advent
opinions.today: Split on 'people who went along with wrong under pressure deserve a full second chance' vs 'they should step down'.

opinions.position: The books of Scripture are a fixed list; add nothing, take nothing away. Some other books may be read by beginners, and the 'apocryphal' books are inventions of heretics.
opinions.side_note: His list of 27 New Testament books is the first exact match to today's.
opinions.quote: Let no man add to these, neither let him take ought from these.
opinions.translation: H. Burgess and J. Payne Smith, NPNF second series vol. 4 (1892), New Advent
opinions.today: Too technical for a disguised statement; good reveal material. Churches still differ on the Old Testament list.

opinions.position: Since Christ rose, death is no longer terrible; Christians, even young ones, can face it without fear.
opinions.side_note: Death is defeated, so fear of it is unnecessary; compare Cyprian on mourning.
opinions.quote: But now that the Saviour has raised His body, death is no longer terrible
opinions.work: On the Incarnation of the Word
opinions.translation: A. Robertson, NPNF second series vol. 4 (1892), New Advent
opinions.today: Split: 'I am not afraid of dying' vs 'death is frightening and it is honest to say so'.

opinions.position: God became human so that humans could be made divine, sharing God's life and immortality.
opinions.side_note: The classic statement of deification (theosis).
opinions.quote: For He was made man that we might be made God
opinions.work: On the Incarnation of the Word
opinions.translation: A. Robertson, NPNF second series vol. 4 (1892), New Advent
opinions.today: Central to Orthodox Christians and embraced by some Catholics; many Protestants find the wording alarming. A reveal line rather than a statement.

opinions.position: A feast is not revelry; the true feast is prayer and thanksgiving. The feasts of those who live for pleasure end in grief.
opinions.side_note: Joy through worship, not indulgence.
opinions.quote: For what else is the feast, but the service of the soul?
opinions.translation: H. Burgess and J. Payne Smith, NPNF second series vol. 4 (1892), New Advent
opinions.today: Split: 'a celebration is about food, drink and fun' vs 'real celebration is gratitude'.

opinions.position: Demons are real and are still driven out wherever Christ's name is spoken; this is proof of who He is.
opinions.side_note: For present-day spiritual power.
opinions.quote: For where the Saviour's name is named, there every demon is driven out.
opinions.work: On the Incarnation of the Word
opinions.translation: A. Robertson, NPNF second series vol. 4 (1892), New Advent
opinions.today: Split: Pentecostals, many Catholics and Orthodox, and global South Christians affirm it; many Western Christians and sceptics do not.

opinions.position: Be careful what you publish: most readers do not look for your meaning, but read your words through envy or a wish to fight, and twist them.
opinions.side_note: He asked the recipient not to copy or share this letter.
opinions.quote: For the majority of men do not consider the faith, or the aim of the writer, but either through envy or a spirit of contention, receive what is written as themselves choose
opinions.work: Letter 54, to Serapion, on the death of Arius
opinions.translation: M. Atkinson and A. Robertson, NPNF second series vol. 4 (1892), New Advent
opinions.today: Very current (social media): 'Most people read you in bad faith, so say less' vs 'Say what you think and let people judge'. Splits people.

sparring.over: Whether the Son of God is a creature. Athanasius refused to readmit him and later wrote a gleeful account of his sudden death in a public latrine as God's judgment.
sparring.source: Letter 54, to Serapion, on the death of Arius; Apology against the Arians 59

sparring.with: Eusebius of Nicomedia and his party
sparring.over: Arius's readmission and Athanasius's deposition; he accuses them of buying the Melitians and inventing charges.
sparring.source: Apology against the Arians 59-60; History of the Arians

sparring.over: Constantine threatened to depose him for refusing Arius, then exiled him to Trier (335) on the grain-ship charge.
sparring.source: Apology against the Arians 59, 87

sparring.over: Imperial control of the church and the Arian cause; Athanasius called him Saul, Ahab and the forerunner of Antichrist.
sparring.source: History of the Arians 33, 52, 67, 77; Apology to Constantius

sparring.over: Julian called him 'that enemy of the gods' and ordered him out of Egypt for baptizing pagan women of rank.
sparring.source: Julian, Letters 46 and 47 (W. C. Wright, 1923)

sparring.over: The rival bishop installed in Alexandria (357) with troops; Athanasius describes the violence of his arrival.
sparring.source: Defence of his Flight 6-7; History of the Arians 75

sparring.over: A rival Egyptian church; they brought the charges of the broken chalice and the murdered Arsenius, and he called them 'dogs unable to forget their vomit'.
sparring.source: Apology against the Arians 59-72; Socrates, Church History 1.27-32

sparring.over: The Council of Alexandria (362), led by Athanasius, received back bishops who had signed under pressure; Lucifer condemned its decisions and his followers became a separate sect. Athanasius's own letters to Lucifer (Letters 50-51) are warm.
sparring.source: Socrates, Church History 3.9; Athanasius, Letter 55 to Rufinianus
